disclaimer: Educational self-help demonstrations of CBT principles. They are not diagnosis, emergency care, or a substitute for appropriate professional treatment.

exercises.title: The 7-Step Thought Record
exercises.purpose: See how a situation, interpretation, emotion and response can be separated and reconsidered.
prompts: Situation: what happened? Keep this as observable as possible.
Feelings/body: what did you notice, and how intense was it?
Automatic thought: what went through your mind?
Evidence for: what facts genuinely support that thought?
Evidence against: what facts do not fit it, or what is missing?
Balanced thought: what interpretation fits the full evidence without forced positivity?
Check again: what changed in emotion, body or intended action?
exercises.mechanism: The exercise slows an automatic interpretation into inspectable parts, then asks whether the first thought explains all the evidence. CBT is not asking you to call a bad situation good; it is testing whether your interpretation is complete and useful.
exercises.not_established: A calmer feeling does not prove the balanced thought is true, and no answer diagnoses a cognitive distortion.

exercises.title: Catch → Check → Change
exercises.purpose: Practise cognitive flexibility when an unhelpful thought arrives quickly.
prompts: Catch it: write the thought in one sentence.
Check it: what is fact, what is prediction, and what other explanations fit?
Change it: write a neutral or more balanced version you can actually believe.
exercises.mechanism: This makes the thought an object of examination rather than an instruction that must be obeyed. The goal is flexible thinking, not cheerful thinking.
exercises.not_established: Some difficult thoughts are accurate. Reframing must not erase danger, grief, discrimination, abuse or material problems.

exercises.title: Map the Loop
exercises.purpose: See how thoughts, feelings and actions can reinforce one another.
prompts: Name the situation.
What did you think or predict?
What emotion or body response followed?
What did you do or avoid doing?
What happened next that may have strengthened or weakened the original thought?
exercises.mechanism: CBT often looks for maintaining loops. If avoidance reduces anxiety for five minutes but makes the feared task larger tomorrow, the short-term relief may be helping maintain the longer-term problem.
exercises.not_established: A loop map is a working formulation, not a diagnosis or proof of cause.

exercises.title: The Tiny Next Step
exercises.purpose: Turn a vague avoided task into one small behaviour that creates momentum or information.
prompts: What are you avoiding or putting off?
What feeling or prediction shows up around it?
What is a step small enough to begin in five minutes?
What will you observe after doing only that step?
exercises.mechanism: Changing behaviour can alter the feedback loop. A small action can produce new evidence and reduce the need to solve the entire future before starting.
exercises.not_established: Starting is not always the right choice. Rest, help, accessibility changes or stopping may be more appropriate.

exercises.title: Problem-Solving Grid
exercises.purpose: Separate a solvable problem from worry about possibilities you cannot currently control.
prompts: Define the problem in concrete terms.
List possible actions without judging them yet.
For each action, note likely benefits, costs and obstacles.
Choose one proportionate next action.
Set a review point: what result will tell you what to do next?
exercises.mechanism: Structure reduces the number of decisions being made at once and turns broad worry into testable action where action is possible.
exercises.not_established: Not every problem is personally solvable, and structural or interpersonal problems should not be reframed as individual thinking errors.

exercises.title: Affect → Action for Cognitive Work
exercises.purpose: Use CBT-style regulation to re-engage coding, study, research, debugging or writing without pretending the emotion is gone.
prompts: Label: what emotion/state is present?
Separate: what is the observable work problem, and what is the prediction or self-judgement?
Reappraise: what balanced interpretation preserves the facts?
Decompose: what is the smallest action that produces information?
Test: do it, then review the result before choosing the next action.
exercises.mechanism: Affect labelling and cognitive reappraisal have been associated with prefrontal/control-system engagement and changes in emotional responding. The practical aim is to make enough reflective space to choose a next action, not to 'move emotion into the prefrontal cortex'.
exercises.not_established: This does not guarantee better productivity, prove a particular neural state, or mean distress should be worked through instead of rested, treated or supported.
